question: Explain John 3:16 in plain language.
localAnswer: John 3:16 teaches that God's love is shown in giving his Son so that those who believe receive eternal life.

evidence.title: John 3:16
evidence.content: John 3:16 connects God's love, the giving of his Son, belief, and eternal life.

question: What are the main theological teachings of Genesis 1?
localAnswer: Genesis 1 presents God as Creator, creation as ordered and good, humanity as made in God's image, and the seventh day as blessed and set apart.

evidence.title: Genesis 1 overview
evidence.content: Genesis 1:1 identifies God as Creator. Genesis 1:27 describes humanity as created in God's image. The chapter repeatedly calls creation good and culminates in divine rest.

mustNotInclude: genesis proves the exact age of the earth

question: Who was Moses and what was his role?
localAnswer: Moses was called by God to lead Israel out of Egypt and became the covenant mediator through whom Israel received the law.

evidence.title: Call of Moses
evidence.content: Exodus 3:10 records God sending Moses to Pharaoh to bring Israel out of Egypt. Moses later serves as Israel's leader and covenant mediator.

question: What does the shepherd imagery in Psalm 23 communicate?
localAnswer: The shepherd imagery portrays the Lord's personal care, guidance, provision, protection, and faithful presence.

evidence.title: Psalm 23
evidence.content: Psalm 23:1 calls the Lord the psalmist's shepherd. The psalm develops themes of provision, guidance, protection, presence, and enduring goodness.

question: Summarize Paul's resurrection argument in 1 Corinthians 15.
localAnswer: Paul treats Christ's resurrection as central to the gospel and as the basis of believers' future bodily resurrection and victory over death.

evidence.title: Resurrection chapter
evidence.content: In 1 Corinthians 15:20 Paul calls the risen Christ the firstfruits of those who have died. The chapter links Christ's resurrection to believers' future resurrection and the defeat of death.

question: Who was the apostle Paul?
localAnswer: Paul, formerly known as Saul, became an apostle of Jesus Christ and a major missionary and letter writer in the early church.

evidence.title: Paul
evidence.content: Acts 9:15 describes Saul as chosen to carry Christ's name. Known as Paul, he became a missionary to Gentiles and wrote letters preserved in the New Testament.

mustNotInclude: one of the twelve disciples during jesus' ministry

question: Why is Ruth important in the biblical story?
localAnswer: Ruth was a Moabite woman whose loyalty to Naomi and faithfulness led to her inclusion in Israel and the family line of David.

evidence.title: Ruth
evidence.content: Ruth 1:16 expresses Ruth's loyalty to Naomi and commitment to Naomi's people and God. Ruth later becomes part of the family line leading to David.

question: What do Christians mean by the Trinity?
localAnswer: The Trinity is the Christian doctrine that the one God eternally exists as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—distinct persons who share the one divine being.

evidence.title: Trinity overview
evidence.content: Matthew 28:19 names Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together. Historic Trinitarian doctrine confesses one God in three distinct persons, not three gods and not one person appearing in three temporary modes.

question: What is justification by faith?
localAnswer: Justification refers to God declaring sinners righteous on the basis of Christ, received through faith rather than earned as a wage.

evidence.title: Justification
evidence.content: Romans 3:28 connects justification with faith apart from works of the law. Christian traditions agree that salvation depends on God's grace in Christ, while differing in how they explain justification's relationship to sanctification and works.

question: Explain the major Christian views of baptism fairly.
localAnswer: Christians agree that baptism is commanded and identifies a person with Christ and the church, but differ over its subjects, mode, and relationship to grace.

evidence.title: Baptism views
evidence.content: Matthew 28:19 includes baptism in disciple-making. Credobaptists baptize professing believers; paedobaptists also baptize children of covenant households. Traditions differ on immersion, pouring, or sprinkling and on whether baptism is primarily symbolic, a covenant sign, or a means of grace.

mustNotInclude: all other views are obviously false

question: How do Christian traditions understand Communion?
localAnswer: Christian traditions agree that Communion remembers and proclaims Christ's death, while differing over how Christ is present and how the sacrament communicates grace.

evidence.title: Lord's Supper
evidence.content: 1 Corinthians 11:26 connects eating and drinking with proclaiming the Lord's death. Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Reformed, and memorialist traditions describe Christ's presence and the sacrament's operation differently.

mustNotInclude: every christian agrees on how christ is present

question: Briefly compare premillennial, amillennial, and postmillennial views.
localAnswer: These views differ over how the millennium and Christ's return relate, while affirming Christ's ultimate victory, resurrection, judgment, and the renewal of creation.

evidence.title: Millennial views
evidence.content: Revelation 20:4 refers to a thousand-year reign. Premillennialism places Christ's return before the millennium; amillennialism interprets the millennium as the present reign of Christ with his saints; postmillennialism anticipates an extended era of gospel blessing before Christ's return.

mustNotInclude: the bible unambiguously settles every millennial detail

question: What does agape mean in New Testament Greek?
localAnswer: Agape is a Greek noun commonly translated love; its precise sense depends on context and it does not by itself guarantee a uniquely divine kind of love.

evidence.title: agape
evidence.content: Strong's G26, agapē, is a Greek noun meaning love, affection, goodwill, or benevolence. Context determines its nuance.

mustNotInclude: always means divine unconditional love and nothing else

question: What does hesed mean in biblical Hebrew?
localAnswer: Hesed is a Hebrew term with a range including steadfast love, covenant loyalty, kindness, and mercy, depending on context.

evidence.title: hesed
evidence.content: Strong's H2617, hesed, can denote kindness, mercy, steadfast love, faithfulness, and covenant loyalty. No single English word captures every use.

mustNotInclude: has only one possible english translation

question: Explain logos in the opening of John's Gospel.
localAnswer: Logos ordinarily means word, message, or reason, but John's opening uses it as a title for the preexistent divine Word who becomes flesh in Jesus Christ.

evidence.title: Logos in John
evidence.content: John 1:1 speaks of the Logos being with God and being God. Strong's G3056 can mean word, statement, message, or reason. John's context gives the term its christological significance.

mustNotInclude: logos always refers to jesus in every greek text

question: Why was the Council of Nicaea important?
localAnswer: The Council of Nicaea addressed the Arian controversy and confessed that the Son is truly divine and of the same essence as the Father; it did not invent belief in Jesus' divinity.

evidence.title: Council of Nicaea
evidence.content: The Council of Nicaea met in AD 325 amid controversy over Arius's teaching. Its creed confessed the Son as begotten, not made, and of the same essence as the Father. The council clarified an existing controversy rather than creating Christianity or selecting the biblical canon.

mustNotInclude: nicaea chose the books of the bible

question: What does Apocrypha or Deuterocanonical books mean?
localAnswer: The terms refer to a collection of ancient Jewish writings whose canonical status differs among Christian traditions; Catholic and Orthodox canons include books that most Protestants classify as Apocrypha.

evidence.title: Apocrypha overview
evidence.content: Deuterocanonical is common Catholic terminology for certain Old Testament books. Protestant Bibles generally label these writings Apocrypha and do not treat them as canonical Scripture. Orthodox canons include overlapping collections with some differences.

mustNotInclude: all christians have exactly the same old testament canon

question: What exact year was the book of Hebrews written?
localAnswer: The exact year is unknown. Many scholars place Hebrews before or around the destruction of Jerusalem, but the evidence does not establish a precise date.

evidence.title: Hebrews background
evidence.content: Hebrews does not identify a writing date. Proposals vary, and internal evidence does not prove an exact year.

question: I am grieving. Can SHARP replace talking with my pastor or a counselor?
localAnswer: SHARP can offer biblical study support, but it cannot replace compassionate human care from trusted pastors, counselors, family, or friends.

evidence.title: SHARP boundaries
evidence.content: SHARP is a Bible and app research assistant. It is not a pastor, therapist, emergency service, or substitute for trusted human care.
